Adopting a light strip

A strip is the first thing this house adopts that is neither a bridge nor already in a wall. Four of its five beats are the sheet the panel already ships; the fifth has no precedent, and A, B and C are three whole answers to it. Every screen is 1440×900, the size of the wall.

WHY THIS EXISTS

A light strip is the first thing this house has been asked to adopt that is not a bridge and not already in a wall. It is bought in a box, taped behind a television or under a shelf, and plugged into a socket that is nowhere near the hub.

The decision taken before these boards: it is NEVER carried to the hub on a cable. It leaves the factory flashed, so it can knock the moment it has power. design/puck/Knock.dc.html argued exactly this shape for the bridge and lost on one line -- "it only works on a bridge that already has firmware on it". A product we ship is flashed. That objection is gone, and docs/puck-hardware.md's open question is answered for this device class.

So most of this collection is not a proposal. It is a demonstration that a strip already fits the sheet the house has. There is exactly one moment with no precedent, and boards A, B and C are the three whole answers to it.

THE SPINE, AND WHY IT IS SHORT

Five beats. Four of them are somebody else's work, already shipped and already tested on a household.

Beat two gets BETTER rather than merely reused. The puck proves it is the one by blinking a single indicator LED at somebody standing over it. A strip proves it by lighting two meters of itself. There is no list to pick out of, no chip id on a screen, and no failure mode where two arrive at once and the wall has to describe them.

THE LIGHT'S PRECEDENCE DOES NOT CARRY OVER, and this is worth writing down before anybody copies the table out of docs/puck-light.md. For a puck a fault outranks everything, because a puck that glows while its bridge is down is furniture that lies. A strip is the opposite case: the household is watching a film, and a strip that turns amber mid-scene because the broker blinked is the product breaking, not reporting. Here the light stays what the person set it to, and the panel carries the fault.

OPEN: which end is the first light. It does not matter for a wash and matters completely for a sweep, and no board here asks it. Probably it is not a question at all -- a sweep that runs the wrong way is fixed by one "other way round" on the tile, which is a thing you can judge by looking rather than a thing you have to answer in advance.

THE ONE QUESTION WITH NO PRECEDENT

The controller cannot know how long the strip is. Nobody can tell it but the household, and the household bought a light, not a component -- they do not know the number and should never have to.

What makes this genuinely hard is that the strip cannot show you what it does not have. Write three hundred lights to a strip of a hundred and eighty and the extra two hundred and twenty fall off the end of the wire, invisibly. So every design that works by "look at where the light is" only has information in one direction, and that asymmetry is what separates these three.

A first draft of A had a single light TRAVELING down the strip, to be tapped when it reached the end. It is drawn here as a fill instead, because a traveling head goes invisible the moment it passes the real end and there is nothing left to tap. A fill stops changing at exactly that moment, which is the thing a person can actually catch.

CHOSEN, 20 SEPTEMBER 2026 -- A AT SETUP, B AFTERWARDS

A -- IT FILLS, AND YOU STOP IT

The lights come on one at a time from the plug end. The person watches the actual strip, not the screen, and taps once when the far end lights.

FOR: one tap, no number, no measuring, nothing to understand. It is the same idea as pressing a switch to say which room it is in -- you identify a thing by doing something to it and watching what happens. And it is self-correcting by construction: the moment the fill stops changing IS the answer, so a person who taps a beat late is a few lights out and a person who taps early sees dark at the end and does it again.

AGAINST: it is timed, and timing is the one thing a wall panel is bad at asking for. Somebody who looked away misses it and has to sit through another pass. It also assumes the strip is in view of the panel, which behind a television it usually is, and under a kitchen shelf it may not be.

OPEN: how fast. Slow enough to catch is slow enough to be boring at five meters; the board has a Slower button, which is an admission that one speed may not do.

TAKEN TOGETHER WITH B rather than instead of it. The fill is the setup moment, because it is one tap and asks for no number; the trim handle lives on the strip's own pane for anybody who cut it down, joined another on, or answered wrong. They are not a fork -- they are the same fact, asked once while somebody is standing there and editable for ever after.

CHOSEN AS THE SECOND HALF -- IT LIVES ON THE PANE, NOT IN SETUP

B -- ALL OF IT IS LIT, AND YOU TRIM IT BACK

Everything is on. Drag the handle back until the dark part is about to appear.

FOR: nothing is timed. The person can take as long as they like, look away, come back, and the strip is still saying the same thing. It is also the only one of the three that can be re-done casually afterwards, which matters when somebody cuts a strip down or joins two together -- and people do both.

AGAINST: it is a search, not an answer, and it is a search in the dark in one direction. Dragging the handle PAST the real end shows nothing at all, so the person has to overshoot, come back, and find the edge by feel. The board hides this behind a plain-words readout, and that readout is the tell: it is there because the picture alone does not close the question.

AND IT PUTS A NUMBER ON THE WALL. "About 3.1 m" is friendlier than a count of lights, but it is still a measurement in a product whose whole argument is that you never take one.

Everything the AGAINST says is true of B as a setup beat and mostly harmless as an afterwards control: a person going looking for it has already decided something is wrong, so a search is what they came for, and the readout they were not to be shown at setup is the thing they want now.

NOT CHOSEN -- KEPT, WITH ITS CASE INTACT

C -- IT NEVER ASKS

Write a generous number of lights every frame and let the surplus fall off the end of the wire. On, off, brighter, dimmer, any color: all correct on any strip, with nothing asked and nothing to get wrong.

FOR: it is the shortest setup of the three by an entire beat, and it is the only one that cannot be done wrong. For the product as described -- accent lighting, a shelf, the back of a television, warm and on -- it is very possibly the whole of the right answer.

AGAINST: anything that needs to know where the middle is comes out wrong, and the board draws that rather than describing it. A wash meant to run the width of the shelf finishes early and the remainder sits on one color.

THE REAL ARGUMENT IS ABOUT THE SECOND PRODUCT. If following the television picture is where this is going, the length is not optional -- the zones are defined in terms of it -- and C does not remove the question, it defers it to the worst possible moment: months later, to a household that already believes the thing is set up. Choosing C is a bet that the ambient light and the picture follower are genuinely two products and not one.

What decided it: the bet at the foot of the board is a bet about whether the picture follower is a separate product, and that is not settled. A is one tap, so C's advantage over it was one tap's worth -- too little to buy a deferred question with.

WHAT WAS DECIDED, AND WHAT IT COST

20 September 2026: A at setup, B afterwards on the pane. C stays on the canvas with its case intact, because the argument it makes -- that the ambient light and the picture follower are two products and the second one's questions should not be charged to the first -- is still live and will come back.

The two boards below were drawn after that decision, not before it. Later is what choosing two answers rather than one actually costs: a surface that has to hold both of them for ever. Order is a question nobody had asked yet, and it is the more dangerous of the two, because a strip whose red is green is broken in a way the household can see and the panel cannot.

THE ORDER THE COLORS COME IN

Raised 20 September, and it is a real hole in everything above: strips do not agree on which channel goes down the wire first. WS2812B is green-red-blue, plenty of others are red-green-blue, and there are six orderings in circulation.

IT CANNOT BE DETECTED. The data line is write-only -- there is no readback on any of these parts -- so the controller can never ask a strip what it wants. It has to be told, and the two obvious ways of telling it are both wrong: asking the household in those words is exactly the component vocabulary product-direction-out-of-the-box forbids, and guessing silently ships a product whose red is not red.

So it is shown. The strip is lit red and the household says what they see, which is the same move as pressing a switch to say which room it is in. The common strip is already right and answers in one tap; a second question only ever reaches the households whose first answer was no, and two primaries settle all six orderings between them, because whichever color comes back names the channel that went out first.

THE FOURTH CHOICE IS THE INTERESTING ONE. A three-byte frame sent to a strip that carries a separate white channel misaligns by a byte a pixel and comes out as a repeating candy-stripe rather than one color. So "stripes" answers a completely different question -- how many channels -- without a word of vocabulary, and it is the one answer on the board that nobody has to be taught to give.

WRITING THE CODE FOUND A SUBTLETY THE BOARD GLOSSES. "One tap" is a prior, not a proof. The first question makes the SECOND byte loud, so the channel somebody names is the one that byte drives -- and that always leaves two orderings standing, never one. Answering "yes, red" leaves grb and brg, and we take grb because it is what almost every 5 V strip on sale actually is. So the row on the light's own pane is not a nicety: it is the other half of this shortcut, and the shortcut is not honest without it. resolve() in brain/hub/strip.py says the same thing where somebody changing it would see it, and a test pins that the first answer always leaves a pair.

AFTERWARDS -- BOTH ANSWERS, ON ITS OWN PANE

The consequence of choosing A and B together, and of the color question existing at all: two things were settled once, while somebody stood in front of the strip, and both of them go stale.

A strip gets cut down to fit a shelf. Another gets soldered on to reach round a corner. One fails and is replaced by whatever was in stock, which is very often not the same make and therefore not the same channel order. None of that is unusual and none of it should mean setting the thing up again.

So the pane carries both, and carries them quietly: everything above the two rows is the ordinary light pane, drawn by LightPane.vue with no knowledge that this is a strip. The strip-shaped part is two rows at the foot of the cluster, and each one is the setup question it came from, reopened.

NOTE WHAT IS NOT HERE. No effects list, no segments, no zones. A strip with a hundred named animations is a maker's toy; this is an accent light that a household should be able to forget about. If the picture follower ever ships, it arrives as its own thing and argues for its own screens.

WHERE THE SETUP CODE COMES FROM

The question the firmware move left behind, and the one thing between a commissionable strip and a household owning one. Matter's advertisement carries a discriminator and NEVER the passcode -- that is the standard being careful, not an oversight -- so something outside the radio has to bring it, and the hub cannot invent it.

IT IS A QUESTION ABOUT design/puck/Knock.dc.html AS MUCH AS ABOUT A STRIP. That board's proudest line is that the identity check is the object and never a number: no chip id, no serial, nothing to read out to anybody. A passcode is a number. So whichever of these wins, Knock either survives, is bought back at a price, or is amended -- and it should be amended deliberately rather than quietly eroded by a protocol.

B IS THE ONE THAT LOOKS BEST AND IS PROBABLY WRONG, which is why it is drawn rather than described. It keeps the one-tap promise exactly, and it does it by making every unit we sell commissionable by anybody who has worked out the derivation -- from a serial that is in the advertisement, using a secret that is in every hub we ship. It also fails certification, which forbids a passcode with a fixed relationship to anything public. A thing can be the nicest screen here and still not be shippable.

A IS WHAT EVERY OTHER MAKER DOES and is finished, honest and dull. C is the interesting middle: the proof becomes physical rather than written, Knock's argument mostly survives, and the cost is that a wall panel cannot do it at all -- which in a house whose every other setup happens on the wall is a real thing to give up.

THE ANSWER MAY BE OUTSIDE THESE THREE. It usually has been.
